analysis.summary: Enforces sorted import declarations by member syntax type and then by identifier name.
firingShapes: import x from './mod';\nimport * as ns from './mod';
silentShapes: import * as ns1 from './mod';\nimport * as ns2 from './mod'
analysis.fixDescription: Reorders top-level import declarations so they are grouped by member syntax in the configured order (none, all, multiple, single) and sorted lexicographically within each group by the first imported identifier or alias; also sorts the members inside multiple-import braces alphabetically.
hazards: Moving a side-effect-only import ('import "mod"') after another import may change execution order if the moved module depends on bindings from the later module.

Placing a namespace import ('import * as ns') before a named import from the same module can cause a temporal dead zone if the named import is accessed during the namespace module's top-level execution.
Swapping two named imports from different modules may break code if one module relies on a global side effect of the other that happens during its evaluation.
Changing the order of imports can affect which duplicate binding wins in environments with non-strict or sloppy mode due to conflicting let/const/var declarations across modules.

If an import is used in a dynamic import() expression later in the file, moving it earlier does not change behavior but moving it later could cause a reference error if the dynamic import relies on it being hoisted.

Relocating an import that supplies a value used in a default export statement may temporarily leave the export undefined during module evaluation if the export statement runs before the import is moved.
Altering import order can interfere with tools that rely on comment positioning for metadata (e.g., @ts-ignore, eslint-disable-next-line) if comments are attached to import lines and get reordered.

In CommonJS interop scenarios, reordering ES imports may change the shape of the namespace object if the target module conditionally exports based on __dirname or process.argv evaluated at import time.
Moving a type-only import (when using TypeScript's import type) after a value import from the same module may break if the type import was relied upon to avoid triggering side effects.
If an import statement has an inline comment that affects tooling (e.g., // @ts-nocheck), moving that line may remove the comment's scope, altering type-checking behavior.
Swapping imports can change the order of __esModule getter invocations when interoperating with default exports from CommonJS modules, potentially affecting which property is considered the default.
If two modules define identically named bindings and the later one is moved before the former, any reference to that binding will now resolve to the earlier module's value, changing semantics.
